title: Assignment 20 · Express and constructive conditions
summary: Express and constructive conditions. Assigned readings and principal cases for this class.
notes:
Luttinger v. Rosen: A home buyer who diligently sought the specified mortgage could recover the deposit when no qualifying loan was available; the seller’s later offer to subsidize a different loan did not satisfy the condition.

Peacock Construction Co. v. Modern Air Conditioning, Inc.: An ambiguous subcontract payment clause set a time for payment rather than transferring the owner’s insolvency risk to the subcontractors.

Gibson v. Cranage: A buyer who had expressly reserved personal satisfaction with a portrait of his deceased daughter was not required to pay merely because others might regard the portrait as excellent.

Kingston v. Preston: An apprentice had to provide the agreed security for payment before he could compel the transfer of his employer’s business.

Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent: An innocent substitution of equivalent pipe could be substantial performance; the owner’s monetary allowance depended on the significance of the defect and the disproportionate cost of replacement.

Gill v. Johnstown Lumber Co.: A log-driving contract was divisible by completed deliveries at specified unit prices, but the contractor could not collect a fraction of a delivery price for logs lost partway through the journey.

Nelson v. Hazel: A negligent builder who had not substantially performed could recover the net benefit retained by the homeowner after credit for payments and the cost of correcting defects.

McKenna v. Vernon: An owner who repeatedly paid without the architect’s required certificate could not invoke the absent final certificate to defeat payment for honestly and substantially completed work.
